name: Anterior thalamic nucleus
function: Anterior thalamic nuclear group participating in hippocampal-diencephalic memory circuits. It receives mammillary input through the mammillothalamic tract, direct hippocampal/subicular inputs through the fornix, and cortical feedback; outputs reach cingulate/retrosplenial limbic cortex.

afferent: Mammillary bodies through the mammillothalamic tract
efferent: Cingulate and retrosplenial limbic cortex

bloodSupply: Tuberothalamic (polar) artery, usually arising from the posterior communicating artery; paramedian PCA supply may substitute when this vessel is absent.

clinical.findings: Acute anterograde amnesia, apathy, abulia and executive dysfunction; left-sided lesions add an 'aphasia-plus' state and right-sided lesions neglect, because the Papez circuit is interrupted at the anterior nucleus.
Thiamine deficiency damages the anterior thalamic nuclei together with the mammillary bodies, producing dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Ventral anterior nucleus (VA)
function: Motor gating hub of the basal-ganglia thalamocortical loop: pallidal (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata output relays here before reaching premotor and supplementary motor cortex, shaping motor readiness and movement initiation.

afferent: Globus pallidus internus via the ansa lenticularis and the lenticular (H2) / thalamic (H1) fasciculi
Premotor and supplementary motor cortex feedback
efferent: Premotor cortex (area 6) and supplementary motor area via the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Frontal eye field region (magnocellular medial VA)

bloodSupply: Tuberothalamic (anterior thalamoperforating) artery rostrally; paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches of the PCA medially.

clinical.findings: VA-region lesions may contribute to disturbed movement initiation and executive behavior when neighboring thalamofrontal networks are involved. Thalamic astasia and active pusher behavior are different clinical phenomena and do not localize uniquely to VA.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Ventral lateral nucleus (VL)
function: Motor thalamic relay for cerebellar and basal-ganglia inputs. Cerebellar output mainly reaches posterior VL (VLp/VL pars caudalis), while pallidal inputs preferentially reach more anterior motor-thalamic territories; nomenclature differs across atlases. The VIM region is a functional-neurosurgical tremor target.

afferent: Contralateral dentate (and interposed) nuclei via the superior cerebellar peduncle and its decussation
Globus pallidus internus via the thalamic fasciculus (H1)
efferent: Primary motor cortex (area 4) and premotor/supplementary motor areas via the posterior limb of the internal capsule

bloodSupply: Inferolateral (thalamogeniculate) PCA branches and variable tuberothalamic/posterior-communicating contributions rostrally.

clinical.findings: VL infarction disconnects the dentatothalamocortical loop, producing contralateral intention tremor, dysmetria and ataxic gait; the same circuit is the target of VIM thalamotomy/DBS for Parkinsonian and essential tremor.
clinical.note: cerebellar-type signs from a thalamic lesion: the dentatothalamic relay, not the cerebellum itself, is interrupted

clinical.syndrome: Ataxic hemiparesis from a thalamic lacune
clinical.findings: A small thalamogeniculate infarct can involve VL together with the adjacent posterior-limb fibres of the internal capsule, giving mild contralateral weakness with out-of-proportion limb ataxia, and trunk instability severe enough to prevent standing (thalamic astasia); at the bedside the picture is indistinguishable from a pontine or capsular lacune.
clinical.note: Ataxic hemiparesis is a syndrome of site, not of cause: identical presentations arise from lacunes in the internal capsule, basis pontis and thalamus, so imaging decides the level.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL)
function: Major thalamic relay for contralateral body somatosensation, including medial-lemniscal vibration/position/discriminative-touch inputs and anterolateral inputs. It projects mainly to somatosensory cortex with broad leg-lateral/arm-more-medial topography. Pain processing also uses other thalamic and cortical routes, so VPL is not an obligatory relay for every aspect of body sensation.

afferent: Medial lemniscus (contralateral dorsal column-medial lemniscus system: vibration, proprioception, discriminative touch)
efferent: Primary somatosensory cortex (S1, areas 3, 1, 2) via the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Secondary somatosensory cortex and insular nociceptive matrix

bloodSupply: PCA — thalamogeniculate artery (branch of the P2 segment).

clinical.findings: VPL injury can cause contralateral body sensory loss, sometimes with sensory ataxia. VPM extension may add facial involvement.
Some lesions involving somatosensory pathways develop delayed neuropathic pain, allodynia or hyperpathia. This is not the inevitable evolution of a thalamic sensory infarct.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM)
function: Thalamic relay for the face and head: the trigeminal lemniscus delivers contralateral facial touch, pain and temperature, the dorsal trigeminothalamic tract adds ipsilateral oral mechanosensation, and the parvocellular medial pole (VPMpc) relays taste to the insular and frontal opercular cortex.

afferent: Contralateral ventral trigeminothalamic (trigeminal lemniscus) tract from the principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei
Solitariothalamic taste fibers to VPMpc via the central tegmental tract
efferent: Face region of primary somatosensory cortex (lateral postcentral gyrus, areas 3, 1, 2)
Insular and frontal opercular taste cortex (VPMpc)

bloodSupply: Inferolateral (thalamogeniculate) PCA perforators to the ventral posterior complex, with variable overlap from neighboring thalamic territories.

clinical.findings: VPM injury can impair contralateral facial sensation; small ventral-posterior lesions near the VPM/VPL border may cause contralateral perioral and hand numbness. Corneal blink circuitry lies in the brainstem and can be preserved. Taste dysfunction may occur when gustatory relay regions are involved.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Lateral dorsal nucleus
function: Dorsal-tier limbic association nucleus continuous with the anterior nuclear group: it links hippocampal and pretectal inputs to cingulate and parietal cortex, participating in memory retrieval and spatial-attention circuitry.

afferent: Cingulate and parietal association cortex feedback
efferent: Cingulate gyrus and superior parietal association cortex (areas 5, 7)
Reciprocal projections to the hippocampal formation

bloodSupply: Posterior choroidal (medial and lateral) and thalamogeniculate branches of the PCA.

clinical.findings: Isolated LD infarcts are rare; LD involvement in larger posterior-choroidal strokes contributes to memory impairment and contralateral spatial neglect.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Lateral posterior nucleus
function: Parietal-association relay behind the lateral dorsal nucleus: with the pulvinar it integrates superior-colliculus visual signals with somatosensory association input and projects to parietal cortex, supporting visuospatial attention and orienting.

efferent: Superior parietal association cortex (areas 5 and 7)
Cingulate cortex

bloodSupply: PCA — posterior choroidal and thalamogeniculate branches.

clinical.findings: Right-sided LP/pulvinar lesions impair assignment of stimulus salience and contralateral visual attention, mimicking parietal neglect without cortical damage.
clinical.vascular: PCA — posterior choroidal or thalamogeniculate branches

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Pulvinar
function: Large posterior thalamic association complex with reciprocal parietal, temporal and occipital cortical connections and tectal input. It participates in visual attention and orienting toward relevant stimuli. It is distinct from the ventral posterior primary somatosensory relay and from smaller posterior nociceptive nuclei.

efferent: Parietotemporo-occipital association cortex and additional association networks

bloodSupply: Posterior choroidal and variable inferolateral branches of the PCA. Thalamic blood supply also includes the tuberothalamic artery from the posterior communicating artery and anterior choroidal contributions elsewhere; it is not uniformly a PCA-only system.

clinical.findings: Pulvinar-region lesions can contribute to contralateral visual inattention or neglect. Visual field loss may reflect adjacent geniculate or visual pathway involvement rather than pulvinar injury alone.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Mediodorsal nucleus (MD)
function: Executive relay of the thalamus: the mediodorsal nucleus reciprocally connects the amygdala and temporal limbic cortex with dorsolateral prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex — also carrying nigral and collicular inputs — supporting working memory, decision-making, affective valuation and memory retrieval.

afferent: Superior colliculus (caudal MD) and olfactory-related input
efferent: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (area 46) and orbitofrontal cortex via the anterior limb of the internal capsule
Reciprocal prefrontal projections back to MD

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches including the artery of Percheron when present; anterior choroidal contributions rostrolaterally.

clinical.findings: MD/associated thalamic injury may affect memory, motivation, executive control and behavior. Bilateral paramedian lesions can also affect arousal or gaze circuitry; the full Percheron triad is not attributable solely to MD. Korsakoff memory impairment reflects a broader diencephalic/frontal network.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Centromedian-parafascicular nuclei
function: Caudal intralaminar centromedian-parafascicular nuclear complex within the internal medullary lamina. It has major basal-ganglia/striatal connections and receives reticular and sensory inputs. Rostral intralaminar nuclei (central lateral, paracentral, central medial), which are distinct from this CM-PF record, have particularly important ascending-arousal connections.

afferent: Basal-ganglia, brainstem reticular and sensory inputs
efferent: Striatum and cortical targets; exact projections differ by subdivision

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches, including the artery of Percheron when present.

clinical.findings: Bilateral paramedian thalamic injury can affect arousal, attention and memory. Those effects involve a broader rostral intralaminar/midline/mediodorsal network and should not be attributed solely to CM-PF.
Intralaminar targets have been studied for epilepsy and disorders of consciousness; such target studies do not establish a specific isolated human lesion syndrome.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Midline (paraventricular) thalamic nuclei
function: Midline limbic nuclei on the walls of the third ventricle (paraventricular, rhomboid, reuniens groups): they connect hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray and amygdala with limbic cortex, mediating nonspecific arousal, stress responsiveness and autonomic-endocrine integration.

afferent: Periaqueductal gray and brainstem reticular formation
efferent: Anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex
Amygdala, hippocampus and entorhinal cortex (reciprocal)

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches; posterior choroidal arteries caudally.

clinical.findings: Midline, rostral intralaminar and mediodorsal network injury can affect arousal, memory and behavior. Severity varies from sleepiness to severe consciousness impairment; a given EEG or structurally normal cortex is not a required signature.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Thalamic reticular nucleus
function: Thin GABAergic sheet between the dorsal thalamus and internal capsule. It receives thalamocortical/corticothalamic collaterals and modulatory inputs and returns inhibition to thalamic nuclei, participating in sensory gating, attention and sleep oscillations. Unlike dorsal-thalamic relay nuclei, it has no direct cortical output.

afferent: Basal forebrain and brainstem cholinergic, serotonergic and noradrenergic modulators
efferent: Inhibitory (GABAergic) projections to the dorsal thalamic relay nuclei — no cortical projection

bloodSupply: Anterior choroidal artery and thalamogeniculate/posterior choroidal branches of the PCA (lateral thalamic rim).

clinical.findings: Reticular and relay neurons participate in sleep spindles and thalamocortical rhythms, including circuitry relevant to absence epilepsy. These phenomena arise from distributed networks rather than an isolated TRN lesion. Fatal familial insomnia predominantly involves other thalamic nuclei and is not a canonical selective TRN lesion syndrome.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).
Cortelli et al., Fatal familial insomnia: sleep, neuroendocrine and vegetative alterations, 1994, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7795890/ (predominant thalamic degeneration).

name: Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)
function: Obligatory relay of retinal vision to cortex: six layers receive a strictly retinotopic, eye-segregated map (ipsilateral eye 2/3/5, contralateral 1/4/6), with magnocellular layers serving motion and parvocellular layers form and color, forwarded to V1 via the retrolenticular internal capsule. Pupil-light-reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN, so LGN lesions spare the light reflex.

afferent: Retinal ganglion cells via the optic tract (M-layers: motion; P-layers: form/color; koniocellular layers: blue-yellow)
Pulvinar, superior colliculus and brainstem attention/arousal modulators
efferent: Primary visual cortex (V1, area 17) via the retrolenticular internal capsule (optic radiations)

bloodSupply: Anterior choroidal artery (anterior and lateral LGN) and lateral posterior choroidal branch of the PCA (posterior and hilar LGN) — a dual supply.

clinical.findings: LGN lesions can produce contralateral homonymous hemianopia or sector defects. Anterior-choroidal injury may produce upper/lower sector loss sparing the horizontal meridian; lateral-posterior-choroidal injury may produce a horizontal wedge defect. Vascular patterns overlap and are not mutually exclusive rules. Pupillary light pathways can be spared because retinal light-reflex fibers bypass the LGN.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, LGN layers and visual relays, printed pp. 464-466 (PDF pp. 490-492).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, visual pathway vascular supply, printed pp. 476-477 (PDF pp. 502-503).
Helgason et al., Anterior choroidal artery-territory infarction, Arch Neurol 1986, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3729746/.

name: Medial geniculate nucleus (MGN)
function: Thalamic relay of audition: the tonotopically organized medial geniculate body receives the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects through the sublenticular internal capsule to Heschl's gyrus — ventral division for frequency analysis, dorsal (polymodal) and medial divisions for sound salience, arousal and multimodal integration.

afferent: Inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus (terminal of the lateral lemniscus system)
Reticular activating system input to the medial division
efferent: Primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus, areas 41/42) via the sublenticular internal capsule (auditory radiations)

bloodSupply: PCA — thalamogeniculate branch, with anterior choroidal contributions to the medial pole.

clinical.findings: An isolated unilateral MGN lesion usually does not cause complete unilateral deafness because each side receives bilateral auditory information. Bilateral central auditory lesions can severely impair hearing; pure word deafness and cortical deafness refer to broader auditory cortical/connection syndromes and should not be inferred automatically from an MGN label.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, central auditory pathways, printed pp. 521-523 (PDF pp. 547-549).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic relays, printed pp. 284-285 (PDF pp. 310-311).

name: Internal medullary lamina
function: Y-shaped intrathalamic white-matter sheet partitioning anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups, with intralaminar nuclei embedded in it. It is an anatomical partition rather than an independent neuronal relay or a uniquely established source of hypertensive hemorrhage.
contextNote: Context record: white-matter lamina tagged on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-thalamus; not a functional nucleus — see the individual thalamic nucleus records.

afferent: Intralaminar fibers of the embedded centromedian-parafascicular nuclei
Fibers crossing between the nuclear groups it separates
efferent: Intralaminar projections to striatum and widespread cortex via the embedded nuclei

bloodSupply: PCA — paramedian and thalamogeniculate perforating branches (intrathalamic perforators).

clinical.findings: Lesions extending across the internal medullary lamina may affect several thalamic nuclear groups and combine sensory, motor, memory or arousal deficits. Hemorrhage and intraventricular extension depend on the involved vessels and lesion extent.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
Schmahmann, Vascular Syndromes of the Thalamus, Stroke 2003;34:2264-2278, https://doi.org/10.1161/01.STR.0000087786.38997.9E (arterial origin and territorial variability).

name: Thalamus (context envelope)
function: Context representation of paired ovoid thalami flanking the third ventricle. An interthalamic adhesion is present in many people but varies and may be absent; it is not a major functional commissure. The atlas silhouette is schematic and the individual nuclei have separate records.
contextNote: Envelope/block tag for the thalamus silhouette on sagittal and coronal plates and in the 3D scene; not a nucleus record (see the 14 individual thalamic nucleus records).

afferent: All thalamocortical, corticothalamic, cerebellar, pallidal, retinal, auditory and somatosensory afferents listed in the individual nucleus records
efferent: Layered cortical projections through the internal capsule (see individual nuclei)

bloodSupply: Tuberothalamic branches from posterior communicating artery; paramedian, inferolateral/thalamogeniculate and posterior choroidal branches mainly from PCA; variable anterior choroidal contributions.

clinical.findings: Bilateral medial thalamic lesions can produce altered arousal, memory dysfunction and vertical gaze abnormalities, sometimes from artery-of-Percheron occlusion.

Astasia is inability to maintain stance disproportionate to weakness. Contraversive pushing is a distinct active postural behavior associated with posterior thalamic and other lesions; it should not be conflated with every thalamic standing deficit.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, thalamic nuclei, Table 7.3 and Figs. 7.6-7.8, printed pp. 283-287 (PDF pp. 309-313).
